WHAT COPYRIGHT PROTECTS, AND THE IDEA/EXPRESSION DISTINCTION
Federal copyright law defines what copyright protects, and where that protection stops, in a single statutory provision. Under 17 U.S.C. § 102(a), copyright protection "subsists, in accordance with this title, in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device," and the statute lists eight illustrative categories, including literary, musical, dramatic, choreographic, pictorial/graphic/sculptural, audiovisual, sound-recording, and architectural works. The same section immediately limits that protection: under § 102(b), "[i]n no case does copyright protection for an original work of authorship extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in such work." Copyright can accordingly protect the particular expression fixed in a work — the specific words, images, or sounds an author actually created — without protecting the underlying idea, method, system, or discovery that expression describes, no matter how that idea or method is written down. The work identified in this document, Riverbend (novel), is described here as: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

THE BASIC TERM OF COPYRIGHT PROTECTION
Federal copyright law fixes the basic term of protection based on when a work was created and, for certain categories, on how the work is attributed rather than on who the individual human author is. Under 17 U.S.C. § 302(a), for a work created on or after January 1, 1978, copyright "subsists from its creation and, except as provided by the following subsections, endures for a term consisting of the life of the author and 70 years after the author's death." A joint work created by co-authors who did not work for hire instead runs for the life of the last surviving co-author plus 70 years, under § 302(b). A different, fixed-duration rule applies to three specific categories the statute treats alike: under § 302(c), "[i]n the case of an anonymous work, a pseudonymous work, or a work made for hire, the copyright endures for a term of 95 years from the year of its first publication, or a term of 120 years from the year of its creation, whichever expires first." Which of these rules actually measures the term of a given work's copyright turns on how that work is attributed and, for a work made for hire, on whether it in fact qualifies as one under the statutory definition of that term — a categorization this document does not make for Riverbend (novel).

REGISTRATION IS OPTIONAL, NOT A CONDITION OF COPYRIGHT PROTECTION
Federal law makes registering a copyright with the U.S. Copyright Office optional, not a prerequisite to copyright existing in the first place. Under 17 U.S.C. § 408(a), the owner of copyright in a work "may obtain registration of the copyright claim" at any time during the copyright's subsistence, by delivering the required deposit, application, and fee to the Copyright Office — and the statute states directly that "[s]uch registration is not a condition of copyright protection." Copyright itself arises automatically, under the originality and fixation rules described elsewhere in this document, the moment an eligible work is created and fixed in a tangible medium; registering it with the Copyright Office afterward is a separate, optional step, taken (or not taken) for reasons — including the benefits and deadlines described in the other clauses of this document — that are independent of whether the copyright itself exists.

DEPOSIT AND APPLICATION REQUIREMENTS FOR REGISTRATION
Registering a copyright requires delivering specific physical or digital material to the Copyright Office, not just completing a form. Under 17 U.S.C. § 408(b), the material that must be deposited for registration depends on the work's publication status: "the material deposited for registration shall include" — for an unpublished work, one complete copy or phonorecord; for a published work, two complete copies or phonorecords of the best edition; for a work first published outside the United States, one complete copy or phonorecord as so published; and for a contribution to a collective work, one complete copy or phonorecord of the best edition of the collective work. This deposit requirement applies in addition to the application and fee that § 408(a) separately requires before the Copyright Office will register a claim. The Register of Copyrights is separately authorized to adjust these default deposit requirements by regulation for particular administrative classes of works.

THE CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION AND ITS EVIDENTIARY EFFECT IN COURT
Once the Copyright Office grants registration, federal law gives the resulting certificate a specific legal effect in litigation, but that effect depends on timing. Under 17 U.S.C. § 410(a), after examining the deposited material and confirming the other legal and formal requirements are met, "the Register shall register the claim and issue to the applicant a certificate of registration under the seal of the Copyright Office," stating the information from the application along with the registration's number and effective date. Under § 410(c), "the certificate of a registration made before or within five years after first publication of the work shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright and of the facts stated in the certificate. The evidentiary weight to be accorded the certificate of a registration made thereafter shall be within the discretion of the court." A timely certificate accordingly shifts an initial evidentiary presumption in the certificate holder's favor; a later one does not carry that same automatic presumption, and how much weight a court gives it is left to the court's own discretion.

REGISTRATION (OR ITS REFUSAL) AS A PRECONDITION TO AN INFRINGEMENT LAWSUIT
Owning a copyright and being able to sue someone for infringing it are not the same thing under federal law — a further statutory step generally has to happen first. Under 17 U.S.C. § 411(a), with narrow exceptions, "no civil action for infringement of the copyright in any United States work shall be instituted until preregistration or registration of the copyright claim has been made in accordance with this title." That step does not require the Copyright Office to have granted registration, however: the same subsection provides that where the deposit, application, and fee required for registration have been delivered to the Copyright Office in proper form and registration has been refused, the applicant is entitled to institute a civil action for infringement if notice of that action is served on the Register of Copyrights. The Supreme Court has confirmed what "registration...has been made" actually means for this purpose: in Fourth Estate Public Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, LLC, the Court unanimously held that "[r]egistration occurs, and a copyright claimant may commence an infringement suit, when the Copyright Office registers a copyright. Upon registration of the copyright, however, a copyright owner can recover for infringement that occurred both before and after registration." Filing an application alone is accordingly not enough to satisfy § 411(a) — the Copyright Office must actually have acted, by registering the claim or by refusing it, before an infringement lawsuit for a United States work can be filed (subject to the statute's own narrow exceptions, including for live transmissions, addressed elsewhere in this document).

THE SAFE-HARBOR TIMING RULE FOR STATUTORY DAMAGES AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
Separately from § 411(a)'s precondition to suing at all, federal law ties two specific remedies to the timing of registration relative to infringement and publication. Under 17 U.S.C. § 412, with narrow exceptions, "no award of statutory damages or of attorney's fees, as provided by sections 504 and 505, shall be made for" (1) "any infringement of copyright in an unpublished work commenced before the effective date of its registration," or (2) "any infringement of copyright commenced after first publication of the work and before the effective date of its registration, unless such registration is made within three months after the first publication of the work." In other words: for an unpublished work, statutory damages and attorney's fees are unavailable for infringement that began before the work's registration became effective; for a published work, they are unavailable for infringement that began after publication and before the effective date of registration, unless the registration's effective date falls within three months after that first publication. A copyright owner can still register later and still sue for infringement under § 411(a) even outside this window — § 412 does not affect whether a suit can be brought, only whether statutory damages and attorney's fees, as opposed to actual damages and the infringer's profits, are available as remedies in it.

Under 17 U.S.C. § 410(a), after examining the deposited material and confirming the other legal and formal requirements are met, "the Register shall register the claim and issue to the applicant a certificate of registration under the seal of the Copyright Office," stating the information from the application along with the registration's number and effective date. Under § 410(c), "the certificate of a registration made before or within five years after first publication of the work shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity of the copyright and of the facts stated in the certificate. The evidentiary weight to be accorded the certificate of a registration made thereafter shall be within the discretion of the court." A timely certificate accordingly shifts an initial evidentiary presumption in the certificate holder's favor; a later one does not carry that same automatic presumption, and how much weight a court gives it is left to the court's own discretion.

expectedJSON.body: Owning a copyright and being able to sue someone for infringing it are not the same thing under federal law — a further statutory step generally has to happen first. Under 17 U.S.C. § 411(a), with narrow exceptions, "no civil action for infringement of the copyright in any United States work shall be instituted until preregistration or registration of the copyright claim has been made in accordance with this title." That step does not require the Copyright Office to have granted registration, however: the same subsection provides that where the deposit, application, and fee required for registration have been delivered to the Copyright Office in proper form and registration has been refused, the applicant is entitled to institute a civil action for infringement if notice of that action is served on the Register of Copyrights. The Supreme Court has confirmed what "registration...has been made" actually means for this purpose: in Fourth Estate Public Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, LLC, the Court unanimously held that "[r]egistration occurs, and a copyright claimant may commence an infringement suit, when the Copyright Office registers a copyright. Upon registration of the copyright, however, a copyright owner can recover for infringement that occurred both before and after registration." Filing an application alone is accordingly not enough to satisfy § 411(a) — the Copyright Office must actually have acted, by registering the claim or by refusing it, before an infringement lawsuit for a United States work can be filed (subject to the statute's own narrow exceptions, including for live transmissions, addressed elsewhere in this document).

expectedJSON.body: Separately from § 411(a)'s precondition to suing at all, federal law ties two specific remedies to the timing of registration relative to infringement and publication. Under 17 U.S.C. § 412, with narrow exceptions, "no award of statutory damages or of attorney's fees, as provided by sections 504 and 505, shall be made for" (1) "any infringement of copyright in an unpublished work commenced before the effective date of its registration," or (2) "any infringement of copyright commenced after first publication of the work and before the effective date of its registration, unless such registration is made within three months after the first publication of the work." In other words: for an unpublished work, statutory damages and attorney's fees are unavailable for infringement that began before the work's registration became effective; for a published work, they are unavailable for infringement that began after publication and before the effective date of registration, unless the registration's effective date falls within three months after that first publication. A copyright owner can still register later and still sue for infringement under § 411(a) even outside this window — § 412 does not affect whether a suit can be brought, only whether statutory damages and attorney's fees, as opposed to actual damages and the infringer's profits, are available as remedies in it.
